title: Three vows (ch. 58)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sick first: in Benedict's Rule, care of the sick comes before all things, because they are served as Christ. Your line was before all things.

Don't make it easy to get in. That's roughly how chapter fifty-eight of Saint Benedict's Rule greets newcomers who ask to join. The one who asks is left waiting, and has to put up with a little rudeness at the door, to see if he means it. If he keeps asking, he's let in, first to the guest house, then to the novices. The Rule itself is read aloud to him, more than once: this is the law you want to serve under. If you can keep it, come in. If not, you are free to go. Today, the promise he makes at the end of all that.
screen: `ENTRY NOT MADE EASY.` → `THE RULE READ TO HIM, AGAIN.` → `IF YOU CAN KEEP IT, COME IN.`

segments.voice: When the time comes, the novice stands before the whole community in the oratory, the place of prayer, and promises three things: stability, conversion of life, and obedience. Obedience had its own day earlier. Today is the first one, stability: binding yourself to one community, in one place, for life. A monk doesn't go looking for a better monastery when this one gets hard. He stays with these brothers, this abbot, this kitchen, this choir. In the Rule's first chapter, Benedict has sharp words for monks who wander from house to house. Stability is his answer to that restlessness. Conversion of life is harder to pin down. The Latin phrase is unusual, and readers argue over its exact sense. Some hear a promise to live the monastic way of life; others, a promise to keep being changed, day after day. The novice writes his promise out, in his own hand if he can, and lays it on the altar himself. He sings a verse from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Uphold me according to thy word, and I shall live: and let me not be confounded in my expectation." The community sings it back to him. Then he lies at each brother's feet and asks for their prayers, and from that day, the Rule says, he's counted one of them. The first vow isn't about doing anything grand. It's about not leaving. The holiness Benedict has in mind grows in one patch of ground, among the same faces.
screen: `STABILITY, CONVERSION OF LIFE, OBEDIENCE.` · `STABILITY: ONE COMMUNITY, FOR LIFE.` · `THE PROMISE LAID ON THE ALTAR.` · then, large: `UPHOLD ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD, AND I SHALL LIVE.` · then: `THE FIRST VOW IS NOT LEAVING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've already said yes to, a person, a job, a promise, a place, and notice whether part of you has been edging toward the door. Don't fix it; just name it, and for these two minutes, stay. If you pray, say the psalm line slowly: uphold me according to thy word.
Stability. The first of the three promises in Benedict's Rule: binding yourself to one community and one place, and staying. Today's word.
Your line: stay. Of Benedict's three promises, it's the first and the plainest. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns make their vows of stability, conversion of life and obedience during Mass or in the community's church, and the written promise is placed on the altar, as the Rule describes.

chat.says: Monks take a vow of stability? Is that about staying calm?
options: It's a promise to stay with one community, in one place, for life, not moving on when it gets hard.
It's a promise to keep their feelings steady and never let anger or sadness show during prayer.
It's a promise to keep exactly the same daily schedule forever, whatever monastery they end up in.
chat.meaning: Stability binds a monk to one community and one place for life. Benedict set it against restless monks who wandered from house to house.

notes: The Rule is paraphrased throughout. Check the summary of ch. 58: entry not made easy; newcomer left to knock and bear harsh words; guest house, then novices' quarters; the Rule read to him repeatedly with 'here is the law… if you can keep it, enter; if not, freely depart'; promise of stability, conversatio morum and obedience in the oratory; written petition in his own hand laid on the altar; the Suscipe verse (Ps 118:116) sung and answered by the community; prostration at each brother's feet; counted as one of the community from that day. Specific counts in the Rule (days of knocking, months of reading, how often the verse is sung) were deliberately left out.
Ch. 1's criticism of wandering monks (gyrovagues) is summarized, not named. Confirm.
Conversatio morum: presented as debated, with two readings offered without ranking. Confirm the phrasing 'readers have long argued' is fair.
'Obedience we met a few days ago' refers to day 1192. howItsDone: confirm the description of profession practice.
